lesson.title: How People Live
lesson.summary: Homes around the world, how food gets from the farm to our plate, and how travel and daily life have changed.
learning_objectives: Describe different kinds of homes and why they differ
Follow food from farm to plate
Compare transport and life long ago with today

standards.text: Changes within living memory, where appropriate, aspects of change in national life

success_criteria: I can name different kinds of homes
I can tell the journey of a roti from the farm
I can say how travel and life have changed
lesson.real_life: Seeing a farm or a mill, riding a bus or train, and asking grandparents what life was like when they were small.

blocks.markdown:
A **home** is a place where we live and feel safe.

Homes can be houses, **flats**, **tents** or mud-brick homes.
blocks.say: Where do you live? Your home is the place where you sleep, eat and feel safe. But homes are not all the same! Some families live in houses made of bricks. Some live in flats, high up in a tall building. Some people, who move from place to place, live in tents. And in many villages, families live in homes made of mud bricks. Every one of these is a home.

blocks.markdown:
People build homes to suit the **weather** and what is nearby.

A steep roof lets snow slide off. Thick walls keep a home cool.
blocks.say: Why do homes look different in different places? Because of the weather, and because of what is nearby. In a snowy place, a house often has a steep roof. The heavy snow slides off. In a very hot place, a home has thick walls and shady spaces. They keep the heat out. A home keeps us warm, cool, dry and safe, whatever the weather.

blocks.markdown:
A **farmer** grows food in a **field**.

When the wheat is ready, the farmer cuts it. This is the **harvest**.
blocks.say: Have you ever wondered where your roti comes from? It starts on a farm! A farmer plants wheat seeds in a field. The sun shines and the rain falls. The seeds grow into tall golden wheat. When the wheat is ready, the farmer cuts it. That is called the harvest.

scenes.caption: The seed grows into wheat.
scenes.say: The sun shines, the rain falls, and the seed grows into golden wheat.

scenes.say: Then comes the harvest. The farmer cuts the wheat, with a tractor or a sickle.

question.prompt: What do we call cutting the wheat when it is ready?
question.hint: It happens at the end of the growing time.
question.explanation: Harvest means cutting the crop when it is ready.

blocks.markdown:
The **mill** grinds wheat into **flour**.

Flour and water make **dough**. Cooked dough becomes a roti.
blocks.say: Now the wheat goes on a journey. A lorry takes it to a mill. The mill grinds the wheat into a soft powder called flour. Then someone mixes the flour with water to make dough. The dough is rolled flat and cooked on a hot tawa. And now we have a roti, ready to eat!

blocks.markdown:
Long ago, people travelled on foot or rode **camels** and horses.

Then came trains and cars, and now aeroplanes. Ways of travelling are called **transport**.
blocks.say: How do you get to school? Maybe by car, by bus or on foot. Long ago, there were no cars. People walked, or rode on camels and horses. Others sat in carts pulled by animals. Then trains came, with big engines and long carriages. Later came cars, and then aeroplanes that fly across the sky.

scenes.say: After that came cars and buses. Today we also fly in aeroplanes. A very long journey takes only a few hours!

blocks.markdown:
Older people remember life **long ago**. This is **living memory**.

Their stories show how life has changed.
blocks.say: Here is a secret way to find out about the past. Ask your grandparents, or an older person in your family! They remember what life was like when they were small. What they remember is called living memory. Their stories show us how life has changed.

blocks.markdown:
Many things have **changed**. A telephone used to have a wire. Today we carry mobile phones.

Some things stay the same: families share meals and children play.
blocks.say: Lots of things have changed. When your grandparents were small, many families had only one telephone. It had a wire. Some had no television. Today we can talk to someone far away on a mobile phone. We can even see them on a screen! Some things have not changed at all. Families still share meals, and children still love to play.

blocks.caption: A telephone with a wire long ago, and a mobile phone today.
blocks.say: Look at these two telephones. One has a wire, and one fits in your pocket. That is how much things have changed!
